1.pericope_label: My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king... Thine arrows are sharp in the heart of the king’s enemies

schools.summary: Work on the words. Ellicott calls 'inditing' 'a most unhappy rendering' of a verb meaning to boil or bubble over, corrects the article to 'a king', prefers 'gird on thy hero's sword', and restores the fifth verse's original clause order. Delitzsch reports the ancient Messianic reading and the Targum's 'O King Messiah'.

Read the psalm as type and antitype. Calvin holds it composed concerning Solomon, but that 'whatever excellence had been seen in Solomon had a higher application'; Gill addresses Christ throughout, limiting the praised beauty to the human nature since divine beauty 'admits of no comparison'.

Clarke names Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter as the occasion, then concedes verse by verse that the language outruns him — of the everlasting blessing, of the girded sword, of the prosperous riding alike; Wesley argues from fit, that the praise is 'most true of Christ; but not of Solomon'.

Spurgeon reads the doubled Hebrew as 'Beautiful, beautiful art thou' and hears the poet's heat, since 'heartless hymns are insults to heaven'; Henry takes the title's lilies for the flowers of a nuptial solemnity and refers them to Christ.

Augustine builds on the title's 'things that shall be changed', reading it of a world that has changed from idols to God, and of each believer changed 'from an infidel to a believer: from a thief to a giver of alms'.

debates.question: Who is the king the psalm celebrates?

positions.view: Solomon, primarily — a nuptial song for his marriage to Pharaoh's daughter, carrying a prophetic reference beyond itself.
Christ. The Epistle to the Hebrews assumes it, the Targum already reads 'O King Messiah', and the praise fits no son of David otherwise.

debates.question: What does the title's first word mean?

positions.view: Lilies or roses, 'strewed, with other flowers, at nuptial solemnities' — though he allows the six-stringed instrument as an alternative.
The six-stringed instrument. 'A world of labor has been spent to prove that these lilies mean the saints', and 'I cannot believe that any such meaning is intended.'

debates.question: Who speaks the body of the psalm?

positions.view: The bride's companions, who describe the bridegroom first and then address her.
The poet, interrupted by 'the acclaim of his hearers' — the misplaced 'therefore' marking where their refrain breaks in.

outliers.view: The only voice to make the title's 'things that shall be changed' the subject of the exposition, reading in it the emptying of the temples and the filling of the churches.

themes: My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer.
Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever.
Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O most mighty, with thy glory and thy majesty.
And in thy majesty ride prosperously because of truth and meekness and righteousness; and thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things.
Thine arrows are sharp in the heart of the king’s enemies; whereby the people fall under thee.

6.pericope_label: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever... upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir

schools.summary: Ellicott alone declines the vocative, holding that the Christian application 'does not help us to explain how the monarch... could be addressed as God', and offering 'thy divine throne' or 'Thy throne is of God for ever'. He places the anointing in the wedding ceremony, takes 'fellows' for the groomsmen, and reads the honourable women as harem favourites and the queen as 'stationed' in the procession. Delitzsch marks the turn from hero to bridegroom.

Gill forbids the alternative renderings by name — the words 'will not bear' to be turned into 'thy throne is God' or 'God shall establish thy throne' — and spiritualises the perfumed garments as the human nature, the robe of righteousness, or the people themselves.

Clarke rests the case on the apostle who quoted it and defends the vocative from Attic usage; he reads the oil as proof that mourning is over and the ivory palaces as inlaid wardrobes; Wesley argues from the unbroken address that the king here called God cannot be Solomon.

Henry assigns the speech — 'it is God the Father that says to the Son here' — and takes the sceptre's rightness as exactness, the administration being 'exactly according to the eternal counsel and will of God'.

debates.question: How can the king be addressed as God?

positions.view: He cannot, as the text stands. Render 'thy divine throne', or better 'Thy throne is of God for ever', which is 'grammatically preferable'.
The vocative stands. The words 'will not bear' the alternatives; the nominative serves as vocative; and the address has not changed hands since the first verse.

debates.question: Who are the 'fellows' above whom he is anointed?

positions.view: 'The paranymphs, or attendants on the bridegroom' — the anointing being part of the Oriental marriage proceedings.
'All that ever were anointed for priests or prophets, or kings.'

outliers.view: The only voice to refuse the received 'Thy throne, O God' and propose grammatical alternatives to it.

themes: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.
Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.
All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia, out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad.
Kings’ daughters were among thy honourable women: upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir.

10.pericope_label: Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear... the rich among the people shall intreat thy favour

schools.summary: Ellicott is terse where others expand — the address 'now turns to the bride', worship means 'literally, bow down' — but rearranges the Tyre verse and answers the objection that Tyre was never subject to Israel, the gifts being 'complimentary presents', not tribute. Delitzsch warns that the poet 'combines on the canvas of one picture things that lie wide apart both as to time and place'.

Gill leaves the speaker undetermined among four candidates, and makes the desired beauty wholly derived: 'not natural, nor acquired by her, but what is given her', and 'perfect through the comeliness of her Lord upon her'.

Clarke gives the historical scene and its transfer together — 'forget therefore thy own people, the Egyptians, and take the Israelites in their place', which taken of Christ becomes an address to the Gentiles; Wesley reduces the hard command to one word, 'comparatively', and hears the speaker as a spiritual father.

Henry makes the three verbs a method of profiting by the word, and presses the forgetting against mixed religion; Spurgeon bends the whole mind to the hearing — 'lean forward that no syllable may be unheard' — while bounding the renunciation to 'ties of the sinful nature'.

positions.view: Undecided among four: the psalmist, the King himself, the Father, or the honourable women.
The bride's companions, turning from the bridegroom to their mistress.
The prophet, speaking 'like an elder person, and as her spiritual father and counsellor'.
God, who 'said to the Son, Thy throne is for ever and ever', now saying this to the church.

debates.question: How absolute is the command to forget?

positions.view: Comparative. Family is to be loved less than Christ; 'not that natural ties are broken by grace, but ties of the sinful nature'.
Absolute as to religion: converts must 'wholly cast out the old leaven', or produce 'such a mongrel religion in Christianity as the Samaritans had'.

outliers.view: The only voice to state the limit of the renunciation explicitly, distinguishing natural ties from sinful ones before demanding the break.

themes: Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear; forget also thine own people, and thy father’s house;
So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty: for he is thy Lord; and worship thou him.
And the daughter of Tyre shall be there with a gift; even the rich among the people shall intreat thy favour.

13.pericope_label: The king’s daughter is all glorious within... therefore shall the people praise thee for ever and ever

schools.summary: Ellicott takes 'within' spatially and says so against the tradition — the next clause 'would alone dismiss the reference to moral qualities from which has sprung such a wealth of mystic interpretation' — locates the bride in her own apartments since the procession has not arrived, makes wrought gold woven textures, and turns the raiment of needlework into carpets spread for the procession. Delitzsch holds the contemporary and Messianic senses together without conflict.
Gill keeps both senses of 'within', the inner chamber and the hearts of her members, and takes the promised children for the apostles and then a progeny among the Gentiles.

Clarke supplies the customs — queens who 'scarcely ever appear in public', the enclosed litter in which 'no part of her person is visible' — and holds that the verse about children cannot fit Solomon or his Egyptian queen; Wesley argues the same from the masculine gender of the Hebrew and from the smallness of Solomon's posterity.

Spurgeon reads the glory inwardly, since 'mere skin-deep beauty is nothing in his eyes', and the succession as continuous rather than dynastic: 'the veterans depart, but volunteers fill up the vacant places.'

positions.view: Indoors — in the inner room of the palace, or in the seclusion of the harem. The mystic reading is dismissed by the next clause.
Inwardly — 'within herself', in the heart and secret character; Gill keeps both senses together.

debates.question: What is the raiment of needlework?

positions.view: Not clothing at all: 'this is now more generally understood of rich tapestry carpets spread for the procession'.
The bride's embroidered dress, worn as she is conducted to the bridegroom's house.

debates.question: Who is addressed at 'instead of thy fathers'?

positions.view: The bridegroom — the Hebrew is masculine, and the next verse unquestionably belongs to him.
The bride: 'instead of the kindred, which thou hast left behind in Egypt, thou shalt have numerous children'.

outliers.view: The only voice to remove the bride's embroidered garment from the verse entirely, reading the needlework as carpets laid for the procession to walk on.

themes: The king’s daughter is all glorious within: her clothing is of wrought gold.
She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee.
With gladness and rejoicing shall they be brought: they shall enter into the king’s palace.
Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children, whom thou mayest make princes in all the earth.
I will make thy name to be remembered in all generations: therefore shall the people praise thee for ever and ever.
